questiontext.text:
Goal

Write three functions that convert text to a whole number with try, except, else and finally.

How this works in Python

Java splits exceptions in two. An unchecked one you may ignore. A checked one the compiler will not let you ignore, so the signature has to say so and every caller has to answer for it.

static String load(Path path) throws IOException {
    return Files.readString(path);
}

try {
    String text = load(path);
    record(text);
} catch (IOException e) {
    log(e);
} finally {
    close();
}

Python has no checked exceptions. There is no throws keyword, nothing in a def line says what a function can raise, and no tool stops you from calling it. Python does compile your file to bytecode, and that step checks syntax and nothing whatever about exceptions.

So the compiler will never again hand you a list of what can go wrong. You find out by reading the function, reading its documentation, or reading the code it calls. That cuts both ways. The throws IOException noise is gone, and so is the safety net that produced it.

You have already raised several exceptions without meaning to. int("nope") raises ValueError. A missing key raises KeyError, as the dictionaries topic showed. Hashing a list raises TypeError. Dividing by zero raises ZeroDivisionError. Each of those names is a class, and catching a class catches its subclasses too.

Four keywords cover the shape. try is Java's try. except is Java's catch. finally is Java's finally. Every header ends in a colon and the indented lines under it are the block.

try:
    value = int(text)
except ValueError as exc:
    print("bad value", exc)
finally:
    print("always runs")

except ValueError names the one type you can actually deal with. as exc binds the exception object to a name, which you only need when you want to read it.

The fourth keyword is the one Java has not got. A try may carry an else clause, and it runs when the try block finished without raising anything.

try:
    value = int(text)
except ValueError:
    print("rejected")
else:
    print("accepted")
finally:
    print("logged")

You met that word in the loops topic, where for ... else runs when the loop was never broken out of. Both spellings of else mean the same thing. The normal path completed.

Why bother, when you could put those lines at the bottom of try? Because everything inside try is covered by your except. Park the follow-on work in there instead. A ValueError raised by that follow-on work is then caught by a handler written for the conversion. The handler reports the wrong failure and hides a real one. Keep try down to the line that can fail, and put the work that depends on it in else.

finally runs on every path out of the block, including a return. The return value is worked out first, then finally runs, then the caller gets the value. So a print in finally lands before the caller sees anything.

Your task

Write three functions. None of them is longer than eight lines.

  • strict_reading(text) returns int(text) and handles nothing. Whatever it raises is the caller's problem, and no part of Python records that fact.
  • safe_reading(text, fallback) returns int(text), or fallback when the text is not a whole number.
  • audited_reading(text) converts the text. On ValueError it prints rejected and returns None. Otherwise it prints accepted and returns the number. Either way it prints logged last. Use except, else and finally, one job each.

Watch the order of the printed lines in audited_reading against the order you wrote the clauses in. That is the part worth getting wrong once.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Name the type. except ValueError: and nothing broader. A bare except: and except Exception: are banned in every question of this course.
  • One line inside each try. Only the call that can fail belongs there.
  • The success path goes in else. Do not park it at the bottom of try.
  • Do not inspect the text first. text.isdigit() is the Java reflex, and it answers False for -5 anyway.
  • Leave strict_reading bare. No try, and no comment pretending to be a throws clause.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (strict_reading, safe_reading, audited_reading)) assert "except:" not in whole, "rule broken: no bare except" assert "except Exception" not in whole, "rule broken: catch ValueError by name" audited = inspect.getsource(audited_reading) assert "else:" in audited, "rule broken: the success path belongs in else" assert "finally:" in audited, "rule broken: finally must run on both paths" assert "try:" in inspect.getsource(safe_reading), "rule broken: catch the failure" assert "try:" not in inspect.getsource(strict_reading), "rule broken: strict_reading catches nothing" assert ".isdigit()" not in whole, "rule broken: do not inspect the text first" print(safe_reading("0", -1), safe_reading("-5", -1), safe_reading("", -1)) print(audited_reading("-12"))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write three functions that show a check-then-act lookup breaking and an ask-forgiveness lookup that does not.

How this works in Python

Java trains one shape into you until you stop seeing it. Ask first, then act.

if (readings.containsKey(key)) {
    return readings.get(key);
}
return null;

if (file.exists()) {
    return Files.readString(file.toPath());
}

That style has a name. LBYL, short for "look before you leap". Python's preference has a name too. EAFP, short for "easier to ask forgiveness than permission". You try the operation and you catch the failure.

try:
    return readings[key]
except KeyError:
    return None

Both spellings do the same job when nothing else in the world is running. Three things separate them.

The first is the window. Your check is a statement about the past. Between the check and the act, anything may change the thing you checked. Another thread evicts the key. Another process deletes the file. The check passed and the act fails anyway, and the failure lands in code you wrote on the assumption it could not happen. os.path.exists(p) followed by an open is the classic case, and it is a genuine security bug with its own name in the literature.

The second is cost. Checking costs a second lookup on every call. Setting up a try costs Python close to nothing, and you only pay when something raises. On the happy path EAFP is the cheaper of the two.

The third is honesty. One operation either works or raises. Two operations can disagree with each other.

This is not a ban on checking. if key in readings: on its own reads well and is fine. The rule is narrower. Do not check and then act on the strength of the check.

The other half of this tier is which type you name. except Exception: catches everything your code could ever get wrong. A misspelled name raises NameError. A wrong argument type raises TypeError. A bug you have not written yet raises something you have not thought of. Funnel all of that into one fallback value and a wiring fault becomes a plausible reading.

On a safety-critical system that is worse than a crash. A crash gets investigated. A wrong number gets trusted, averaged, and acted on. Catch the one failure you know how to handle and let the rest travel.

Your task

Your answer box already holds evict. It stands in for whatever else touches the dict while you are working, and it is there to make one of your functions fail.

Write three functions.

  • racy_lookup(readings, key) is the Java shape, written out so you can watch it break. Test whether the key is in readings. If it is, call evict(readings, key), then return readings[key]. Return None when the key was absent.
  • atomic_lookup(readings, key) does the same job in one operation. Subscript inside a try, return None on KeyError, and change nothing.
  • convert_all(rows) walks a list of strings and returns two lists as a pair. The whole numbers it converted, and the strings it could not convert. Catch ValueError and nothing else.

One reading in the tests is 0, and one is the empty string. Both are falsey, as the truth and None topic showed, so anything built on if readings.get(key): reports them as missing. That is the trap.

The tests hand convert_all a list containing None. int(None) raises TypeError, which is not a bad reading, it is a caller who wired the wrong thing in. Your narrow except lets it through to them, which is the correct behaviour.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • except Exception: and bare except: appear nowhere. Name the one type you can handle.
  • atomic_lookup performs one operation. No in, no .get(, no len().
  • convert_all catches ValueError alone. A TypeError is the caller's fault and must reach the caller.
  • Leave evict exactly as it is. It is there to fail, and repairing it removes the lesson.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

testcode.text: import inspect import re whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (racy_lookup, atomic_lookup, convert_all)) assert "except:" not in whole, "rule broken: no bare except" assert "except Exception" not in whole, "rule broken: name the type you can handle" atomic = inspect.getsource(atomic_lookup) assert not re.search(r"\bin\b", atomic), "rule broken: atomic_lookup checks nothing first" assert ".get(" not in atomic, "rule broken: subscript inside try, not .get" assert "len(" not in atomic, "rule broken: one operation only" assert "try:" in atomic, "rule broken: ask forgiveness" assert re.search(r"\bin\b", inspect.getsource(racy_lookup)), "rule broken: keep the check-then-act shape" assert "del " in inspect.getsource(evict), "rule broken: leave evict alone" print(convert_all(["1", "x", "3"])) try: convert_all(["1", None]) except TypeError as exc: print("escaped:", type(exc).__name__) print(convert_all([])) print(atomic_lookup({}, "psi"), atomic_lookup({"psi": ""}, "psi") == "")

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write four functions that turn every low-level failure into a chained SensorFault.

How this works in Python

A Java exception of your own is a small ceremony.

public class SensorFaultException extends Exception {
    public SensorFaultException(String message, Throwable cause) {
        super(message, cause);
    }
}

throw new SensorFaultException("bad channel", e);

Python asks for two lines.

class SensorFault(Exception):
    pass

class is Java's class. The name in brackets is what it inherits from, so that line reads as extends Exception. pass is the empty body, needed because Python has no braces to leave empty. You inherit the message argument, the printable form, and everything else, so an empty body is the normal shape for an exception. Classes proper come later in the course. These two lines are all you need today.

Python names them without the Exception suffix, because except SensorFault: already reads as one.

To keep the cause, write raise ... from.

try:
    raw = config[name]
except KeyError as exc:
    raise SensorFault(f"unknown channel {name!r}") from exc

That is new SensorFaultException(msg, e). The original lands on exc.__cause__. A printed traceback then shows both, joined by the line "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception". Drop the from and you destroy the only record of what actually failed. On a system that has to be explainable after an incident, that is evidence tampering.

The !r conversion in that f-string is the one from the f-strings topic. It puts the quotes round the channel name.

To pass a failure onward untouched, write raise on its own.

except SensorFault:
    print("logging this")
    raise

Java writes throw e there. A bare raise continues the throw already in progress, with its cause and its traceback intact. raise exc starts a fresh throw of the same object and adds a frame that never happened.

Now the part that decides how you write every handler for the rest of your career. Python's exception tree has BaseException at the root. Exception sits under it, and everything you would ever want to handle sits under Exception. Two things deliberately do not. KeyboardInterrupt, which is Ctrl-C, and SystemExit, which is what sys.exit() raises.

They were put outside Exception so that except Exception: cannot swallow them. A bare except: catches BaseException, so it catches both. Write one inside a loop and you have built a program that cannot be stopped from the keyboard and ignores its own shutdown. That is why a bare except: is always wrong, and why except Exception: is nearly always wrong as well.

issubclass(A, B) answers whether A is a subclass of B, so you can check that claim rather than take it on trust.

Last, the reason all of this matters here. When a safety-critical system finds bad state, the correct move is to stop. Continuing turns one bad reading into a plausible average that somebody acts on. Fail loudly.

Your task

SensorFault is already in the answer box. Write four functions under it. config maps a channel name to a string reading.

  • read_channel(config, name) returns the reading as an int. A missing channel becomes SensorFault with the message unknown channel 'depth', chained from the KeyError. A reading that will not convert becomes SensorFault with the message channel 'flow' sent 'n/a', chained from the ValueError. Both names are rendered with !r.
  • checked_read(config, name) calls read_channel, prints fault logged for 'flow' when it fails, and lets the same fault carry on to the caller.
  • commit(config, names) adds up every channel in names, collecting the message from each fault as it goes. If any channel failed it raises SensorFault reading 2 of 3 channels bad: followed by the collected messages joined with "; ". Otherwise it returns the total. Never a partial total.
  • hierarchy() takes no arguments and returns three answers as a tuple. Whether KeyboardInterrupt is a subclass of Exception, whether it is a subclass of BaseException, and whether SensorFault is a subclass of Exception.

Read the first two answers from hierarchy together. They are the whole argument against the bare except: in one line of output.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Nothing but SensorFault leaves your functions. KeyError and ValueError are implementation detail and must not reach the caller.
  • Chain every one with raise ... from exc. A cause thrown away is evidence destroyed.
  • Re-raise with a bare raise on its own line. raise exc is banned.
  • commit raises when any channel is bad. Returning what you managed to add up is the defect this whole topic is about.
  • No bare except: and no except Exception:, here or ever. One of them catches Ctrl-C.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

expected.text: 12 unknown channel 'depth' KeyError channel 'flow' sent 'n/a' ValueError
12 fault logged for 'flow' caller saw: channel 'flow' sent 'n/a' cause survived: ValueError 12 2 of 3 channels bad: channel 'flow' sent 'n/a'; unknown channel 'depth' (False, True, True)

testcode.text: import inspect import re whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(o) for o in (SensorFault, read_channel, checked_read, commit, hierarchy)) assert "except:" not in whole, "rule broken: a bare except also catches KeyboardInterrupt" assert "except Exception" not in whole, "rule broken: catch SensorFault, not everything" assert whole.count("from exc") >= 2, "rule broken: chain every fault with raise ... from" assert re.search(r"\n\s+raise\s*\n", inspect.getsource(checked_read)), "rule broken: re-raise with a bare raise" assert "raise exc" not in whole, "rule broken: a bare raise continues the original throw" assert "KeyError" not in inspect.getsource(commit), "rule broken: commit handles SensorFault only" print(commit({}, [])) print(issubclass(SensorFault, Exception), SensorFault.__mro__[1].__name__) try: commit({"a": "1"}, ["a", "b"]) except SensorFault as exc: print(exc, exc.__cause__) try: read_channel({"a": "1.5"}, "a") except SensorFault as exc: print(exc, type(exc.__cause__).__name__)

expected.text: 0 True Exception 1 of 2 channels bad: unknown channel 'b' None channel 'a' sent '1.5' ValueError
